qualification: NSSCO Economics 6145 (syllabus vNIED 2018; implementation 2019; first examination 2020, examined 2026)

items.prompt: Identify the quantity used in the numerator of PED and the quantity used in the numerator of PES.
items.canonical_answer: Percentage change in quantity demanded for PED; percentage change in quantity supplied for PES.
marking_guidance: Feature (1): quantity demanded percentage. Distinction (1): quantity supplied percentage.
objective_titles: Define price elasticity of demand and supply

items.prompt: Explain the difference between perfectly inelastic demand and demand with PED magnitude 0.5.
items.canonical_answer: Perfectly inelastic demand has no quantity response and PED zero. A magnitude of 0.5 indicates a non-zero quantity response proportionately smaller than the price change.
marking_guidance: Confusion/boundary (1): zero response versus smaller non-zero response. Test to distinguish (1): check whether quantity changes, rather than calling all inelastic demand fixed.
objective_titles: Define price elasticity of demand and supply

items.canonical_answer: The responsiveness of quantity demanded to a price change, measured by percentage change in quantity demanded divided by percentage change in price.
marking_guidance: Meaning/definition and essential element (1): The responsiveness of quantity demanded to a price change, measured by percentage change in quantity demanded divided by percentage change in price.
objective_titles: Describe price elasticity of demand

items.canonical_answer: The responsiveness of quantity supplied to a price change, measured by percentage change in quantity supplied divided by percentage change in price.
marking_guidance: Meaning/definition and essential element (1): The responsiveness of quantity supplied to a price change, measured by percentage change in quantity supplied divided by percentage change in price.
objective_titles: Describe price elasticity of supply

items.prompt: Evaluate a small price increase for an invented seller seeking profit. Demand is estimated to be inelastic over the proposed range, other demand conditions unchanged, but costs and the estimate are uncertain.
items.canonical_answer: Inelastic demand can support a revenue gain because the quantity reduction is proportionately smaller. However, uncertain estimates and costs mean a revenue gain need not become a profit gain. Prefer the increase only if the estimate is relevant and the expected price/quantity outcome covers the cost implications; check actual price-times-quantity figures rather than assume success from the coefficient.
marking_guidance: Argument for (2): inelastic response loses proportionately fewer sales (1), can raise total revenue for small change under stated conditions (1). Argument against (2): estimate uncertain (1), costs can offset revenue gain (1). Condition (1): relevant response and favourable net cost outcome. Judgement (2): conditional support (1), verify actual revenue/cost evidence before claiming profit (1). Total 7.
objective_titles: Discuss and apply price elasticity of demand and supply

items.prompt: Explain how a small price increase can raise total revenue when demand is locally inelastic and other demand conditions are unchanged.
items.canonical_answer: Price per unit rises while quantity demanded falls by a smaller proportion. The gain per unit can outweigh the lost quantity, so price times quantity and total revenue rise under those conditions.
marking_guidance: Starting change (1): price increase. Because/mechanism (1): inelastic quantity reduction proportionately smaller. Link (1): price gain outweighs lost quantity for the small change. Consequence (1): total revenue rises with other demand conditions unchanged. Total 4.
objective_titles: Explain application of price elasticity of demand

items.prompt: Explain the revenue implication in an invented case with unchanged other demand conditions: price rises from N$10 to N$11 and sales fall from 100 to 95, giving inelastic demand.
items.canonical_answer: The relatively small sales reduction is outweighed by the higher price per unit; revenue rises from N$1,000 to N$1,045, though profit still depends on costs.
marking_guidance: Context (1): inelastic response in supplied figures. Reason/consequence (1): price gain outweighs sales loss, raising revenue to N$1,045; no automatic profit claim.
objective_titles: Explain application of price elasticity of demand

items.prompt: Explain how spare capacity and accessible materials can make a producer’s supply more responsive to a higher price in the short run.
items.canonical_answer: The higher price creates an incentive to offer more. Unused equipment time and available materials permit extra output without first building new capacity, so quantity supplied can respond more readily in the period.
marking_guidance: Starting change (1): higher price incentive. Because/mechanism (1): spare equipment capacity. Link (1): accessible materials permit extra production. Consequence (1): stronger quantity-supplied response within the period. Total 4.
objective_titles: Explain application of price elasticity of supply

items.prompt: Explain why supply may be less price responsive for a producer already at full capacity than for one with usable spare equipment and materials.
items.canonical_answer: The constrained producer cannot readily expand output in the period, while the other can use available capacity, so their quantity-supplied responses can differ.
marking_guidance: Context (1): full versus spare capacity. Reason/conclusion (1): differing feasibility of extra output changes responsiveness.
objective_titles: Explain application of price elasticity of supply

items.prompt: Identify the two percentage changes needed to calculate price elasticity of demand.
items.canonical_answer: Percentage change in quantity demanded and percentage change in price.
marking_guidance: Feature (1): quantity demanded percentage. Distinction (1): own-price percentage.
objective_titles: Perform simple calculations of elasticity and inelasticity of demand and supply

items.prompt: Calculate PED magnitude using original bases for an invented market where price rises from N$10 to N$11 and weekly quantity demanded falls from 100 to 95, other demand conditions unchanged.
items.canonical_answer: Quantity proportion = −5/100 = −0.05, equivalent to −5%. Price proportion = 1/10 = 0.1, equivalent to 10%. Using the percentage values, PED = −5/10 = −0.5, magnitude 0.5, inelastic.
marking_guidance: Formula and substitution/working (1): −5% ÷ 10%. Units/interpretation (1): magnitude 0.5, a dimensionless inelastic-demand coefficient. Total 2.
objective_titles: Calculate and interpret calculation of price elasticity of demand

items.prompt: Analyse the meaning of a PED magnitude of 0.5 in an invented market where a 10% price rise is associated with a 5% fall in quantity demanded, other demand conditions unchanged.
items.canonical_answer: The quantity-demanded response is proportionately smaller than the price change, so demand is inelastic. The 5% reduction is still a response, so it is not perfectly inelastic. The estimate describes the stated comparison, not every possible future price.
marking_guidance: Relationship/pattern (1): proportionately smaller quantity response/inelastic. Evidence/comparison (1): 5% versus 10%. Explanation/reason (2): non-zero response distinguishes perfect inelasticity (1), scope restricted to stated comparison (1). Total 4.
objective_titles: Calculate and interpret calculation of price elasticity of demand

items.prompt: Calculate PES using original bases when an invented producer’s price rises from N$20 to N$22 and weekly quantity supplied rises from 50 to 60, other supply conditions unchanged.
items.canonical_answer: Quantity-supplied proportion = 10/50 = 0.2, equivalent to 20%. Price proportion = 2/20 = 0.1, equivalent to 10%. Using the percentage values, PES = 20/10 = 2, elastic.
marking_guidance: Formula and substitution/working (1): 20% ÷ 10%. Units/interpretation (1): coefficient 2, dimensionless and elastic supply. Total 2.
objective_titles: Calculate and interpret calculation of price elasticity of supply

items.prompt: Analyse the meaning of PES 2 when an invented producer supplies 20% more after a 10% own-price rise, other conditions unchanged. Spare capacity is available.
items.canonical_answer: Supply responds proportionately more than price, so it is elastic in the stated period. The 20% versus 10% evidence is consistent with using spare capacity to expand output; it does not establish that every later price rise produces the same coefficient.
marking_guidance: Relationship/pattern (1): elastic supply/proportionately larger Qs response. Evidence/comparison (1): 20% versus 10%. Explanation/reason (2): available capacity permits output response (1), scope limited to stated conditions/period (1). Total 4.
objective_titles: Calculate and interpret calculation of price elasticity of supply

items.prompt: Define price elasticity of demand (2). Identify supply as elastic or inelastic for coefficients 2 and 0.4 respectively (2). Explain one possible total-revenue effect of a small price rise with inelastic demand and unchanged other demand conditions (2). Identify the percentage changes used in this supplied working: price N$10 to N$11 gives 10%; quantity 100 to 95 gives −5% (2).
items.canonical_answer: PED measures percentage quantity-demanded responsiveness to an own-price change. PES2 is elastic; PES0.4 is inelastic. With locally inelastic demand a small price rise can raise revenue as the quantity reduction is proportionately smaller. The supplied changes are price +10% and quantity −5%.
marking_guidance: Meaning (2): responsiveness of quantity demanded (1), percentage Q change divided by percentage price change (1). Separate points for supply types (2): elastic (1), inelastic (1). Explanation (2): smaller proportional quantity loss (1), price gain can raise revenue under stated conditions (1). Identifications (2): price+10% (1), quantity−5% (1). Marks allocation 8.
objective_titles: Describe price elasticity of demand

items.prompt: Invented teaching data, using original bases: a notebook price rises from N$10 to N$11 and weekly quantity demanded changes from 100 to 95, with other demand conditions unchanged. A producer’s price rises from N$20 to N$22 and quantity supplied rises from 50 to 60, with other supply conditions unchanged and spare capacity available. Describe three features of the elasticity calculations (6). Explain the demand and supply coefficients and their economic meaning (7). Discuss a proposed notebook price increase for profit, considering the demand response, costs and the reliability of these estimates (7).
items.canonical_answer: Elasticity uses percentage rather than raw changes, divides quantity response by price change and distinguishes Qd from Qs. The demand calculation gives −5%/10%=−0.5, magnitude0.5 and inelastic; supply gives20%/10%=2 and elastic. Demand changes proportionately less, while spare capacity can support the larger supply response. Notebook revenue changes from N$1,000 to N$1,045 in the supplied case. That supports a revenue argument, but costs and relevance of estimates still determine profit. Prefer the proposed increase only if a credible response and cost assessment support it.
marking_guidance: Context/data description (6): percentage changes (1), original bases stated (1); Q response in numerator (1), price response denominator (1); demand uses Qd (1), supply uses Qs (1). Mechanism/explanation (7): demand−5% (1), price+10% (1), PED magnitude0.5/meaning inelastic (1); supply+20% (1), price+10% (1), PES2/meaning elastic (1); capacity can support supply response (1). Both sides/judgement (7): inelastic demand supports revenue argument (1), actual receipts N$1,045 versus N$1,000 (1); costs may offset gain (1), estimate may not remain relevant (1); condition credible response and cost outcome (1); conditional recommendation (1), no revenue-to-profit guarantee (1). Marks allocation 6+7+7=20.

items.prompt: Evaluate a small price increase in two seven-mark plans for an invented seller seeking revenue while monitoring costs. Case 1: demand magnitude is estimated at 0.5 over the proposed range. Case 2: demand magnitude is estimated at 2 over that range. Other demand conditions are unchanged in each case, but estimates have uncertainty and output must be feasible.
items.canonical_answer: Case 1: inelastic demand means a proportionately smaller quantity loss, supporting a revenue gain for the small change. Costs and estimate uncertainty remain disadvantages; conditional support requires a relevant estimate and acceptable costs. Case 2: elastic demand means a relatively large quantity loss, which tends to reduce revenue after the price rise. A higher price per unit is a possible benefit but may be outweighed. Prefer avoiding the increase for a revenue objective unless stronger evidence changes the expected response; calculate actual endpoints and consider costs before claiming profit.
marking_guidance: Case 1 marks (7): argument for higher price per unit (1), smaller proportional sales loss supports revenue (1); argument against estimate uncertainty (1), cost effects (1); condition relevant locally inelastic response (1); judgement conditionally supports increase (1), distinguishes revenue from profit (1). Case 2 allocation (7): argument for higher price per unit (1), may reduce pressure to supply units (1); argument against larger proportional quantity loss (1), likely revenue reduction under elastic demand (1); condition relevance of response estimate (1); judgement avoids revenue-seeking increase (1), subject to better evidence/actual endpoint check (1). Total 14.
objective_titles: Discuss and apply price elasticity of demand and supply
